title: Short thoughts stimulated by Dawn's response to the seven questions schools need evidence about.
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton responds to a reader, Dawn McMaster, who doubts that many school leaders have the skills or time to be learning-focused because the job is mostly firefighting. He agrees the concern is serious, citing a conference where none of 800 people had worked in a school with its own definition of learning. He then offers six short thoughts: leadership and management differ, firefighting is legitimate but must be proportionate, and some teams adopt firefighting as their real Hedgehog Concept. His central move is to reject the too-busy excuse with arithmetic, arguing that an hour a day in classrooms is one tenth of a working week. He closes with a concrete account of a leadership team that committed to a weekly quota of 30-minute classroom visits and met in order to discuss what they had learned. The message is that a modest, shared, regular habit of looking for learning is feasible and transformative even when practiced imperfectly.
points: Firefighting is a normal part of leadership but becomes a problem when it is the whole job, and some teams even invent fires to keep their identity.
The claim that leaders are too busy to focus on learning is answered by arithmetic: five hours a week of classroom visits is a tenth of a working week.
A leadership team can divide classroom visits by role (more from the non-teaching deputy, fewer from the teaching one) and hold each other to a weekly target.
A Friday lunch to discuss the evidence from the visits turns observation into decisions about teaching, learning and school structures.
Starting at a beginning level is acceptable, because getting better at looking for learning is itself learning.
quotes: Some of you will remember the 800 people at a conference I was attending who had, between them, worked in about 3200 schools. When asked, not one person had worked in a school that even had its own definition of learning.
Leadership may be about doing the right things. Management may be about doing things right.
So, there is nothing wrong with leaders and leadership teams putting out fires. I want to say that because leaders and leadership teams shouldn’t expect to be in fire-free zones.
I’m about to say something that has irritated the heck out of school leaders in many different countries. I don’t believe leadership teams are too busy to focus fully on learning.

We used to spend Friday lunch together talking through what we had learned and what the evidence was telling us about learning, teaching and our school. By the end of an average 12 week term we had made 432 x 30 minute visits.
These visits, huge though they seem in number, didn’t take up even 25% of our time in school. They were transformational.
